passages.happening:
Jesus is still speaking to the Pharisees who threw out the man born blind (9:40-41). He tells them a picture story. Anyone who climbs into the sheepfold some other way, instead of using the gate, is a thief and a robber. “But the one who enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep” (verse 2).

The gatekeeper opens the gate for him. “The sheep listen for his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out” (verse 3). He goes ahead of them, and they follow because they know his voice. They will never follow a stranger. They run from him, because they do not know his voice (verses 4-5).

John adds that the hearers did not understand what Jesus was telling them (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Everyone in Judea knew how sheep were kept. At night they were shut in a fold, a pen with stone walls and one opening. Sometimes several flocks shared one fold, with a gatekeeper on watch. In the morning each shepherd came to the gate and called. His own sheep knew his voice and came out to him, and the others stayed put. Then he walked in front of them to the pasture. He led them. He did not drive them from behind.

The picture would land hard right after chapter 9. The leaders had just thrown a man out of the synagogue. The healed man would not follow them. He had heard another voice, and Jesus had come looking for him by name. The story that follows is about who the true shepherd of God's people is, and who is not.

‘Thief’ and ‘robber’ are strong words. A thief sneaks. A robber uses force. Either way, he comes for what he can take, not for the good of the sheep.

‘Calls his own sheep by name’ is a detail worth stopping on. Shepherds did name their animals. A flock is not a crowd of strangers to its shepherd. Each one is known.
passages.ot: Israel had long called God its shepherd: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1), and, “we are the people of His pasture, the sheep under His care. Today, if you hear His voice” (Psalm 95:7). Moses prayed for a leader “who will go out and come in before them, and who will lead them out and bring them in, so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep without a shepherd” (Numbers 27:17).
passages.asks: Sheep know a voice by hearing it again and again. Faith often works the same way. People come to know Jesus' voice by spending time with his words, until they can tell it from the other voices that call to them. If you are not sure you would know his voice, the place to start is simply to keep listening.

passages.happening:
Since they did not understand, Jesus explains. “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep” (verse 7). Those who came before him were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them (verse 8).

“I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved. He will come in and go out and find pasture” (verse 9).

Then he sets two purposes side by side: “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Jesus now uses the picture in a new way. In the first story he was the shepherd who comes in by the gate. Now he is the gate itself, the one way in to safety and the one way out to pasture. The two pictures do not compete. He is both the way in and the one who leads.

Who are the ‘thieves and robbers’ who came before him? Not Moses and the prophets. Jesus honors them all through John (5:46). He seems to mean those who claimed to lead God's people for their own gain. Some readers think of false messiahs and rebels who promised freedom and brought death. Others think of leaders like those in chapter 9, who used their power to push people out. The words fit both.

‘Come in and go out and find pasture’ echoes the way the Scriptures describe a safe, blessed life, going out to work and coming home in peace (Deuteronomy 28:6; Psalm 121:8). Under the true shepherd the sheep are not locked up. They are kept safe, and they are fed.

‘Life in all its fullness’ is one of the best-known lines in John. It does not promise wealth or an easy road. In John ‘life’ means the life of God himself, shared with people, beginning now and not ended by death (3:16, 17:3).
passages.ot: Moses' prayer in Numbers 27:17 asked for a leader who would ‘go out and come in before them’. The Psalms say of God's people, “we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture” (Psalm 100:3). Ezekiel described the bad shepherds who took and gave nothing: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2).
passages.asks: Some voices come to take. They want your money, your loyalty, your time, your silence, and they leave you emptier than they found you. Jesus says he came to give. A good test of any leader, in a church or anywhere else, is to ask whether the people in their care are being fed or used.

passages.t: The good shepherd lays down his life
passages.happening:
“I am the good shepherd,” Jesus says. “The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep” (verse 11). A hired hand is different. When he sees the wolf coming, he leaves the sheep and runs, and the wolf scatters the flock. He runs because he does not care for the sheep (verses 12-13).

“I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father. And I lay down My life for the sheep” (verses 14-15). Then he looks beyond his hearers: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well, and they will listen to My voice. Then there will be one flock and one shepherd” (verse 16).

He says his life will not be taken from him against his will. “I lay it down of My own accord. I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again” (verse 18).

Once more the crowd is divided (verse 19). Many say, “He is demon-possessed and insane. Why would you listen to Him?” Others reply, “These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
Shepherding was dangerous. David told King Saul he had fought lions and bears to save lambs. A hired hand was not expected to go that far. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, later set the rule for a paid shepherd: he had to fight off one wolf, but an attack by two wolves counted as an accident he could not be blamed for. That is the point of Jesus' picture. A hired man has limits, and no one expects him to die for sheep that are not his. The good shepherd does what no hired hand would do.

The word ‘good’ here means more than kind. It means the true and noble shepherd, the real one, set against all the false ones.

Behind the whole picture stands Ezekiel 34. There God condemned Israel's leaders, the shepherds who fed themselves and let the flock scatter. Then he made a promise: ‘I Myself will search for My flock.’ He also promised one shepherd, ‘My servant David’. When Jesus says ‘I am the good shepherd’, he takes both promises on himself. God would shepherd his people himself, and he would do it through the son of David.

‘Other sheep that are not of this fold’ is read by most Christians as meaning people who were not Jews, Gentiles from every nation who would come to believe. John points the same way later, when he says Jesus would die ‘for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one’ (11:52). ‘One flock’ does not mean one pen. It means one people, gathered from many places, under one shepherd.

‘I lay it down of My own accord’ means the cross will not be an accident or a defeat. No one takes Jesus' life from him. He gives it, and he will take it up again.
passages.ot: Ezekiel 34 is the key. God charged the shepherds: “You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays, or searched for the lost” (Ezekiel 34:4). Then he promised, “Behold, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11), and, “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16). And: “I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them” (Ezekiel 34:23). Isaiah pictured God as a shepherd who “gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart” (Isaiah 40:11), and promised, “I will gather to them still others besides those already gathered” (Isaiah 56:8). David told Saul how he fought for the flock: “whenever a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock, I went after it” (1 Samuel 17:34-35).
passages.asks: Many people have been hurt by shepherds who fed themselves: leaders in churches and elsewhere who used the flock instead of caring for it. If that is part of your story, Ezekiel 34 and John 10 are on your side. God himself condemned those shepherds, and Jesus defined a true shepherd as one who gives his life for the sheep, not one who takes life from them. Your hurt does not mean God was like them. It is the opposite of who he says he is.

passages.t: No one can snatch them out of My hand
passages.happening:
Some time later Jesus is back in Jerusalem for the Feast of Dedication. It is winter, and he is walking in the temple courts in Solomon's Colonnade (verses 22-23). The Jewish leaders gather around him and press him: “How long will You keep us in suspense? If You are the Christ, tell us plainly” (verse 24).

“I already told you,” Jesus replies, “but you did not believe. The works I do in My Father’s name testify on My behalf” (verse 25). They do not believe because they are not his sheep (verse 26).

Then he speaks of those who are: “My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand” (verses 27-28). And he adds, “My Father who has given them to Me is greater than all. No one can snatch them out of My Father’s hand” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The Feast of Dedication is the feast Jews today call Hanukkah, a Hebrew word meaning ‘dedication’. Around 167 BC the Greek king Antiochus IV took Jerusalem's temple and set up a pagan altar in it. A Jewish revolt led by Judas Maccabeus won the city back. In 164 BC they cleansed the temple, built a new altar, and dedicated it again. The book of 1 Maccabees (chapter 4) tells how they celebrated for eight days and decreed that the feast be kept every year. Josephus, the Jewish historian, writing near the end of the first century, says it was called ‘Lights’.

So the setting was full of meaning. The feast remembered a king who called himself a god and defiled God's house, and the leaders who freed God's people. It is no surprise that the question in the air was ‘Are you the Christ?’ People hoped for another deliverer. And at this feast Jesus will be accused of making himself God.

Solomon's Colonnade was a covered walkway along the edge of the temple's outer court, probably on its east side. In winter it gave shelter from the cold. The first Christians later met there (Acts 3:11, 5:12).

‘Tell us plainly’ sounds fair. But Jesus has told them, in words and in works, and they have not believed. Their question is not really a request for more evidence.

‘No one can snatch them’ uses the same Greek verb, harpazō, as the wolf that ‘pounces on’ the sheep in verse 12. The wolf can scatter a flock left by a hired hand. It cannot pull a sheep out of the good shepherd's hand.
passages.ot: In Ezekiel 34 God promises to keep his flock from every predator: “I will save My flock, and they will no longer be prey” (Ezekiel 34:22). In Deuteronomy God says of himself, “there is no one who can deliver from My hand” (Deuteronomy 32:39). Jesus says the same of his own hand and his Father's.
passages.hard:
Can a true believer ever be lost? Christians have answered this question differently for centuries, and each answer is held by faithful churches. The views are given here as their own teachers state them.

Many Reformed and Calvinist churches teach what they call the perseverance of the saints. The Westminster Confession, chapter 17, says that those God has truly called and made holy ‘can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace’. They point to this verse: the sheep will never perish, and no one can snatch them from the hand of the Son or the Father. When someone falls away, they say, it shows he was not truly one of the sheep (1 John 2:19).

Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Wesleyan and Methodist churches, and many others, teach that a believer can fall away. They note that the promise is given to sheep who keep listening and following (verse 27), and that no outside power can take them, while the verse does not speak of a sheep who stops following. They point to the New Testament's warnings, such as “If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away” (15:6).

All sides agree on what the verse most plainly says. The safety of Jesus' sheep rests on his hand and his Father's power, not on their own strength. These notes do not settle the question between them. It is a question faithful Christians have long differed on, open for discussion and not a cause for division.
passages.asks: If you fear that you might slip out of God's hand, notice where Jesus puts the weight. Not on how tightly you hold on, but on whose hand is holding you, and that the Father ‘is greater than all’. Many who worry about being lost are the very people who are still listening for his voice. That listening is itself a mark of his sheep.

passages.t: I and the Father are one
passages.happening:
Jesus says, “I and the Father are one” (verse 30). At once the leaders pick up stones again (verse 31). Jesus asks them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these do you stone Me?” (verse 32). They answer that it is not for a good work “but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, declare Yourself to be God” (verse 33).

Jesus replies from Scripture: “Is it not written in your Law: ‘I have said you are gods’?” (verse 34). If Scripture called people ‘gods’, people to whom God's word came, and Scripture cannot be broken, how can they accuse him of blasphemy, the one the Father set apart and sent into the world, for saying, ‘I am the Son of God’? (verses 35-36).

He tells them to look at his works. If he is not doing his Father's works, they need not believe him. But if he is, then “believe the works themselves, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father” (verse 38). Again they try to seize him, but he escapes (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
In Greek ‘one’ here is hen, a neuter word: ‘one thing’, not ‘one person’. Jesus does not say he and the Father are the same person. He speaks of the Father as someone else, who sent him. But he says they are one. Christian teachers have often pointed out that the verse guards against two mistakes at once: making the Son a different, lesser kind of being, and making Father and Son one person under two names.

The leaders hear a claim to be God. ‘You, who are a man, declare Yourself to be God’ (verse 33). That is why they reach for stones. The Law ordered stoning for blasphemy.

Then Jesus answers with Psalm 82. In that psalm God speaks to others and says, ‘You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.’ Then he warns them that they will die like mortals. His argument works from the smaller to the greater, a way of reasoning Jewish teachers often used. If Scripture could call those people ‘gods’, and Scripture cannot be set aside, why is it blasphemy for the one the Father consecrated and sent to call himself God's Son?

‘Sanctified’, or ‘set apart’, is a striking word at the Feast of Dedication. The feast remembered the day the altar was set apart for God again. Jesus says the Father has set him apart and sent him. The holy place they celebrated was standing in front of them in person.
passages.ot: The psalm reads: “God presides in the divine assembly; He renders judgment among the gods” (Psalm 82:1), and then, “I have said, ‘You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.’ But like mortals you will die, and like rulers you will fall” (Psalm 82:6-7). Behind ‘one’ stands Israel's confession, “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus does not deny it. The Law also ordered stoning for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16).
passages.hard:
Two hard questions sit here.

First, what does ‘I and the Father are one’ mean? Some read it as oneness of purpose and will: the Son does exactly what the Father wants. They point to 17:22, where Jesus prays that his followers ‘may be one as We are one’. Others read it as oneness of being: the Son shares the Father's very nature. They point to the leaders' reaction (verse 33), to ‘the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father’ (verse 38), and to the book's frame, from ‘the Word was God’ (1:1) to Thomas's ‘My Lord and my God’ (20:28). The church came to confess both together: one in will because one in being. The Nicene Creed, in the older English wording printed on this site, confesses the Son as ‘being of one substance with the Father’. This is what the creeds bind all Christians to confess.

Second, is Jesus lowering his claim when he quotes ‘you are gods’, as if to say he is divine only in the way others are? Who the ‘gods’ of Psalm 82 are is debated. Many think they are Israel's human judges, who ruled with God's authority and failed. Others think they are heavenly beings in God's court. Later rabbinic tradition read them as Israel at Sinai, made great by receiving God's word. On any of these readings Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater, and most readers, ancient and modern, conclude that he is not backing down. He goes straight on to say ‘the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father’, and his hearers try again to seize him. They did not hear a smaller claim.
passages.asks: The leaders asked for plain words and then reached for stones when they got them. It is possible to ask God for clarity while already deciding not to accept the answer. Jesus' offer is patient: if you cannot yet believe his words, look at his works. Honest searching starts there.

passages.happening:
Jesus leaves Jerusalem and goes back across the Jordan, to the place where John the Baptist had first baptized, and he stays there (verse 40).

Many people come to him there. They say, “Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true” (verse 41). And John ends the chapter simply: “And many in that place believed in Jesus” (verse 42).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends where the Gospel's story of Jesus began, at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John the Baptist had pointed to him (1:28-29). Where exactly this place was is not certain, as John's book page explains.

The people's words are a quiet tribute to John the Baptist. He worked no miracles. He simply told the truth about Jesus, and in the end his words proved true. That was what he had been sent to do: ‘He came as a witness to testify about the Light’ (1:7).

The contrast with Jerusalem is sharp. In the temple, the leaders picked up stones. Out by the river, where the story began, many believed. Jesus withdraws for a time, but not for long. The next chapter will call him back toward Jerusalem, to a grave in Bethany near the city.
passages.asks: John the Baptist never did a sign. He only pointed to Jesus, faithfully, and years later people found that everything he had said was true. Most faithful lives are like that. They do not dazzle. They point to Jesus, and their words prove true over time.
